cloze.text: The sphenoid foramina {{c1::rotundum}}, {{c1::ovale}} and {{c1::spinosum}} are openings for branches of the trigeminal nerve and vessels.
cloze.extra: Tip: these are essential in understanding nerve pathways for anesthesia.

cloze.text: The foramina rotundum, ovale and spinosum of the sphenoid transmit branches of the {{c1::trigeminal (V)}} nerve and vessels.
cloze.extra: Tip: essential for understanding nerve pathways for anesthesia.

cloze.text: The {{c1::lateral pterygoid plate}} of the sphenoid is the area of origin for the {{c2::lateral pterygoid}} muscle.
cloze.extra: Tip: this muscle assists in opening and shifting the jaw.

cloze.text: The {{c1::ethmoid}} bone is a lightweight, spongy bone between the {{c2::orbits}}, forming part of the nasal cavity and septum.
cloze.extra: Tip: not visible externally but vital to nasal structure.

cloze.text: The {{c1::cribriform plate}} of the ethmoid is a horizontal surface with small holes for the {{c2::olfactory}} nerves.
cloze.extra: Tip: transmits smell from the nose to the brain.

cloze.text: The {{c1::crista galli}} is a vertical projection from the {{c2::cribriform plate}} of the ethmoid.
cloze.extra: Tip: serves as an anchor for brain membranes.

cloze.text: The crista galli of the ethmoid serves as an anchor for the {{c1::brain membranes (meninges)}}.
The {{c1::superior}} and {{c1::middle}} nasal conchae are thin, scroll-like projections of the ethmoid bone into the nasal cavity.
cloze.extra: Tip: they help filter and humidify air.

cloze.text: Unlike the superior and middle conchae (part of the ethmoid), the {{c1::inferior nasal conchae}} are separate {{c2::facial}} bones.
cloze.extra: Don't confuse them.

cloze.text: The {{c1::ethmoid sinuses}} are small air spaces within the ethmoid bone.
cloze.extra: Tip: these can become congested and affect pressure around the eyes.

cloze.text: The {{c1::perpendicular plate}} of the ethmoid descends from the cribriform plate to form the {{c2::superior}} portion of the nasal septum.
cloze.extra: Tip: think of it as the bone that divides the nose top-down.

cloze.text: The nasal septum is completed by the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid joining with the {{c1::vomer}} and {{c2::cartilage}}.
There are {{c1::14}} facial bones.
cloze.extra: Paired (2 each): nasal, lacrimal, palatine, inferior nasal concha, zygomatic, maxilla. Single: mandible, vomer.

cloze.text: The two single (unpaired) facial bones are the {{c1::mandible}} and the {{c1::vomer}}.
cloze.extra: The other 6 facial bones are paired: nasal, lacrimal, palatine, inferior nasal concha, zygomatic, maxilla.

cloze.text: The six paired facial bones: {{c1::nasal}}, {{c2::lacrimal}}, {{c3::palatine}}, {{c4::inferior nasal concha}}, zygomatic and maxilla.
The six paired facial bones: nasal, lacrimal, palatine, inferior nasal concha, {{c1::zygomatic}} and {{c2::maxilla}}.
The {{c1::maxillae}} are irregular bones forming the upper jaw, part of the hard palate, the nasal cavity and the {{c2::floor of the orbits}}.
cloze.extra: Tip: they hold all the upper teeth, shape the midface and articulate with nearly every facial bone.

cloze.text: The {{c1::alveolar process}} of the maxilla houses the sockets for all maxillary teeth.
cloze.extra: Tip: the mandible, in contrast, holds the lower teeth.

cloze.text: The {{c1::anterior nasal spine}} is a midline projection of the maxilla at the base of the nose.
cloze.extra: Tip: often appears as a radiopaque V-shape near the central incisors.

cloze.text: On radiographs, the anterior nasal spine appears as a {{c1::radiopaque}} V-shape near the {{c2::central incisors}}.
The {{c1::maxillary sinus}} is a large air-filled cavity above the {{c2::posterior teeth}}.
cloze.extra: Tip: visible on panoramic and PA radiographs.

cloze.text: Maxillary sinus inflammation can mimic {{c1::molar}} pain.
The {{c1::infraorbital foramen}} is an opening below the orbit for the infraorbital nerve and vessels.
cloze.extra: Tip: target for the infraorbital nerve block.

cloze.text: The {{c1::palatine process}} of the maxilla is a horizontal plate forming the {{c2::anterior two-thirds}} of the hard palate.
The two palatine processes of the maxillae join at the midline at the {{c1::intermaxillary (median palatine)}} suture.
The palatine process of the maxilla articulates {{c1::posteriorly}} with the {{c2::palatine bone}}, which forms the remaining {{c3::posterior one-third}} of the hard palate.
The {{c1::palatine}} bones are {{c2::L}}-shaped bones forming the posterior part of the hard palate and portions of the nasal cavity and orbit.
cloze.extra: Tip: the anterior 2/3 of the hard palate is made of the maxilla.

cloze.text: The {{c1::horizontal plate}} of the palatine bone forms the back portion of the hard palate.
cloze.extra: Tip: joins with the palatine process of the maxilla anteriorly.

cloze.text: The {{c1::vertical (perpendicular) plate}} of the palatine bone extends upward to contribute to the {{c2::lateral wall of the nasal cavity}} and part of the orbit.
The {{c1::greater palatine foramen}} is the opening for the greater palatine nerve and vessels.
cloze.extra: Tip: supplies the hard palate and lingual gingiva of posterior teeth.

cloze.text: The greater palatine nerve supplies the {{c1::hard palate}} and the {{c2::lingual (palatal) gingiva of posterior teeth}}.
Don't confuse the greater palatine foramen (posterior) with the {{c1::nasopalatine (incisive)}} foramen, which is located on the {{c2::anterior}} maxilla.
The {{c1::lesser palatine foramina}} are small openings in the palatine bone that transmit the lesser palatine nerves and vessels.
cloze.extra: Tip: these serve the soft palate and uvula, providing sensation and blood supply to the back of the mouth.

cloze.text: The lesser palatine nerves and vessels serve the {{c1::soft palate}} and {{c1::uvula}}.
The {{c1::mandible}} is a U-shaped bone forming the lower jaw and the {{c2::only movable bone}} of the skull.
cloze.extra: Tip: can dislocate in trauma or TMJ disorders.

cloze.text: The {{c1::alveolar process}} of the mandible houses the sockets for all mandibular teeth.
The {{c1::body}} of the mandible is the {{c2::horizontal}} portion that holds the lower teeth.
cloze.extra: Tip: includes the alveolar process and the mental foramen area.

cloze.text: The {{c1::ramus}} is the {{c2::vertical}} extension on each side of the body of the mandible.
The ramus of the mandible contains the {{c1::coronoid process}} (muscle attachment) and the {{c2::condylar process}} (part of the TMJ).
The {{c1::mental foramen}} is an opening on the outer body of the mandible near the {{c2::premolars}} for the {{c3::mental}} nerve.
cloze.extra: Tip: visible on radiographs.

cloze.text: On radiographs, don't confuse the mental foramen with a {{c1::periapical lesion}}.
The {{c1::mandibular foramen}} is an opening on the {{c2::inner (medial) ramus}} for the {{c3::inferior alveolar}} nerve.
cloze.extra: Tip: landmark for the IA nerve block.

cloze.text: The {{c1::mylohyoid line}} is a ridge on the inner mandible for muscle attachment.
cloze.extra: Tip: it separates the sublingual space above from the submandibular space below.

cloze.text: The mylohyoid line separates the {{c1::sublingual}} space above from the {{c2::submandibular}} space below.
The {{c1::genial tubercles}} are small, paired bony projections on the {{c2::lingual midline}} of the mandible.
The genial tubercles are attachment points for the {{c1::genioglossus}} and {{c1::geniohyoid}} muscles.
On radiographs, the genial tubercles appear as a {{c1::ring-shaped radiopacity}} below the {{c2::mandibular incisors}}.
The {{c1::zygomatic}} bones are irregular bones forming the cheekbones and part of the {{c2::orbital wall}}.
cloze.extra: Tip: you feel them when you touch the sides of your face below the eyes.

cloze.text: The zygomatic arch is formed by the {{c1::zygomatic bone}} and the {{c2::zygomatic process of the temporal bone}}.
cloze.extra: Tip: visible during extraoral exams and imaging.

cloze.text: The zygomatic arch is an important attachment site for the {{c1::masseter}} muscle.
cloze.extra: Crucial for mastication.

cloze.text: The {{c1::infraorbital rim}} of the zygomatic bone contributes to the floor of the orbit, together with the maxilla.
cloze.extra: Tip: landmark for infraorbital nerve blocks.

cloze.text: Trauma at the infraorbital rim can affect sensation to the {{c1::upper lip}}, {{c1::cheek}} and {{c1::maxillary anterior teeth}}.
cloze.extra: These are the areas served by the infraorbital nerve.

cloze.text: The {{c1::nasal}} bones are small rectangular bones forming the {{c2::bridge of the nose}}.
cloze.extra: Tip: you touch these when you pinch the upper part of your nose.

cloze.text: The nasal bones join the {{c1::frontal process of the maxilla}} and the {{c2::frontal bone}}.
cloze.extra: Tip: easily fractured in facial injuries, but usually not visible on intraoral radiographs.

cloze.text: The {{c1::lacrimal}} bones are thin, delicate bones forming part of the {{c2::medial wall of the orbit}}.
cloze.extra: Tip: located at the inner corner of the eye, near the tear duct.

cloze.text: The {{c1::lacrimal fossa}} is a depression that houses the {{c2::lacrimal sac}}.
cloze.extra: Tip: involved in tear drainage.

cloze.text: The {{c1::inferior nasal conchae}} are scroll-like bones projecting from the {{c2::lateral walls}} of the nasal cavity.
cloze.extra: Tip: they warm, moisten and filter the air you breathe in.

cloze.text: The {{c1::vomer}} is a thin, flat bone forming the {{c2::lower (inferior)}} part of the nasal septum.
cloze.extra: Tip: separates the left and right nasal cavities beneath the ethmoid bone.

cloze.text: The vomer articulates with the {{c1::maxillae}} and the {{c1::palatine bones}}.
cloze.extra: Tip: may appear as a vertical midline radiopaque shadow in anterior maxillary radiographs.

cloze.text: In anterior maxillary radiographs, the {{c1::vomer}} may appear as a vertical midline {{c2::radiopaque}} shadow.
The first cervical vertebra (C1) is the {{c1::atlas}}; the second (C2) is the {{c2::axis}}.
The vertebral column regions shown from top to bottom: {{c1::cervical}}, {{c2::thoracic}}, {{c3::lumbar}}.
cloze.extra: There are 7 cervical vertebrae (C1–C7).

cloze.text: The {{c1::atlas (C1)}} is the first cervical vertebra, located just below the skull.
The atlas (C1) is {{c1::ring}}-shaped with no {{c2::body}} or {{c2::spinous process}}.
cloze.extra: Tip: supports the skull like the mythological Atlas.

cloze.text: The atlas articulates with the {{c1::occipital condyles}} at the base of the skull.
cloze.extra: Tip: movement at this joint lets you tilt your head forward and back.

cloze.text: The {{c1::atlanto-occipital}} joint (atlas–skull) allows you to nod "{{c2::yes}}".
The {{c1::axis (C2)}} is the second cervical vertebra, with a vertical projection called the {{c2::dens}}.
The axis acts like a {{c1::pivot}} for the skull — it lets you rotate your head "{{c2::no}}".
The {{c1::dens (odontoid process)}} is a peg-like structure of the axis that fits into the {{c2::atlas}}.
cloze.extra: Tip: instead of a disc, this articulation forms a joint (atlantoaxial).

cloze.text: There is no intervertebral disc between C1 and C2; the dens fitting into the atlas forms the {{c1::atlantoaxial}} joint.
cloze.extra: The book's tip reads "forms the a joint" — the joint is the (median) atlantoaxial joint.

cloze.text: Vertebrae {{c1::C3–C7}} are smaller, stacked vertebrae forming the lower neck.
cloze.extra: Tip: they provide flexibility and support while protecting the spinal cord.

cloze.text: The {{c1::transverse foramina}} of the cervical vertebrae are unique openings for the {{c2::vertebral arteries}}.
cloze.extra: The book's heading reads "Spinous processes and transverse foramina" — the openings for the vertebral arteries are the transverse foramina.

cloze.text: Intervertebral discs are located between each vertebral body from {{c1::C2–C7}} and are made of {{c2::fibrocartilage}}.
cloze.extra: No disc between C1 and C2.

cloze.text: The 4 muscles of mastication: {{c1::masseter}}, {{c2::medial pterygoid}}, {{c3::temporalis}}, {{c4::lateral pterygoid}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: MMTL → Mom Makes Tasty Lasagna (Masseter, Medial pterygoid, Temporalis, Lateral pterygoid).

cloze.text: The muscles of mastication work with the {{c1::TMJ}} to accomplish jaw movement (opening and closing the jaw).
All muscles of mastication are innervated by the {{c1::fifth (V) cranial nerve (trigeminal)}}.
The {{c1::masseter}} is located in the cheek area and runs vertically from the cheekbone to the jaw; action: {{c2::elevates the mandible}}.
Masseter attachments — insertion: {{c1::lateral surface of the ramus/angle of the mandible}}; origin: {{c2::zygomatic arch}}.
The masseter is the thick, band-like, most {{c1::superficial}} muscle of mastication; the {{c2::parotid gland}} lies over it and {{c3::facial nerve}} branches pass through it.
cloze.extra: It can generate up to 200 lbs of force.

cloze.text: The {{c1::masseter}} can generate up to {{c2::200 lbs}} of force.
The {{c1::temporalis}} is a fan-shaped muscle in the temporal fossa; action: {{c2::elevates}} and {{c3::retracts}} the mandible.
Temporalis attachments — insertion: {{c1::coronoid process of the mandible}}; origin: {{c2::temporal fossa}}.
You can feel the {{c1::temporalis}} bulge at the temples when clenching; it is a site of {{c2::Botox}} injections for TMJ relief.
The {{c1::medial pterygoid}} lies deep in the cheek, running vertically on the inner side of the mandible; action: {{c2::elevates}} and {{c2::protrudes}} the jaw.
Medial pterygoid attachments — insertion: {{c1::medial surface of the mandible}}; origin: {{c2::pterygoid fossa of the sphenoid}}.
The medial pterygoid mirrors the {{c1::masseter}} on the inside — together they form a {{c2::sling}} to clamp the jaw shut.
cloze.extra: Vertical orientation, unlike the lateral pterygoid.

cloze.text: The {{c1::lateral pterygoid}} is a deep horizontal muscle under the zygomatic arch; action: {{c2::opens}}, protrudes and shifts the jaw.
Lateral pterygoid attachments — insertion: {{c1::TMJ disc and neck of the condyle}}; origin: {{c2::lateral pterygoid plate (sphenoid)}}.
The {{c1::lateral pterygoid}} is the only muscle of mastication that {{c2::opens}} the jaw.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Medial → say "Me" → you are closing your jaw → medial pterygoid closes. Lateral → say "La" → you are opening your jaw → lateral pterygoid opens.

cloze.text: The lateral pterygoid has {{c1::horizontal}} fiber direction and is involved in {{c2::TMJ disc displacement}} and lateral jaw movement.
Closing the jaw involves the {{c1::masseter}}, {{c1::medial pterygoid}} and {{c1::temporalis}} working together.
cloze.extra: Example of muscles working in pairs or groups.

cloze.text: The muscular system includes {{c1::skeletal}}, {{c1::smooth}} and {{c1::cardiac}} muscles.
cloze.extra: In dentistry, we focus on skeletal muscles.

cloze.text: Skeletal muscles are under {{c1::voluntary}} control and are {{c2::striated}}.
cloze.extra: They work in coordination with bones and joints.

cloze.text: Muscles have an origin and an insertion; movement occurs from the {{c1::insertion}} towards the {{c2::origin}}.
The {{c1::origin}} is a muscle's fixed attachment; the {{c2::insertion}} moves when the muscle contracts.
The {{c1::Frontalis}} (muscle of facial expression) — location: Forehead; action: {{c2::raises eyebrows, wrinkles forehead}}.
cloze.extra: Tip: Used in surprise; creates forehead lines.

cloze.text: Frontalis attachments — insertion: {{c1::skin above eyebrows}}; origin: {{c2::epicranial aponeurosis}}.
Muscle of facial expression: {{c1::Frontalis}} — used in surprise; creates forehead lines.
The {{c1::Orbicularis oculi}} (muscle of facial expression) — location: surrounds eye; action: {{c2::closes eyelid}}.
cloze.extra: Tip: Used in blinking, squinting, winking.

cloze.text: Orbicularis oculi attachments — insertion: {{c1::skin around eye}}; origin: {{c2::orbital rim, frontal bone, maxilla}}.
Muscle of facial expression: {{c1::Orbicularis oculi}} — used in blinking, squinting, winking.
The {{c1::Corrugator supercilii}} (muscle of facial expression) — location: between eyebrows; action: {{c2::draws eyebrows medially/downward}}.
cloze.extra: Tip: Creates vertical frown lines between eyebrows.

cloze.text: Corrugator supercilii attachments — insertion: {{c1::skin of eyebrows}}; origin: {{c2::frontal bone}}.
Muscle of facial expression: {{c1::Corrugator supercilii}} — creates vertical frown lines between eyebrows.
The {{c1::Orbicularis oris}} (muscle of facial expression) — location: around mouth; action: {{c2::closes and puckers lips}}.
cloze.extra: Tip: Kissing muscle; used with straw (drinking), blowing.

cloze.text: Orbicularis oris attachments — insertion: {{c1::skin at lips}}; origin: {{c2::maxilla, mandible, surrounding muscles}}.
Muscle of facial expression: {{c1::Orbicularis oris}} — kissing muscle; used with straw (drinking), blowing.
The {{c1::Buccinator}} (muscle of facial expression) — location: cheek; action: {{c2::compresses cheek}}.
cloze.extra: Tip: Keeps food in mouth; the "trumpet muscle".

cloze.text: Buccinator attachments — insertion: {{c1::mouth corner}}; origin: {{c2::maxilla, mandible, pterygomandibular raphe}}.
Muscle of facial expression: {{c1::Buccinator}} — keeps food in mouth; the "trumpet muscle".
The {{c1::Zygomaticus major}} (muscle of facial expression) — location: cheek to mouth corner; action: {{c2::elevates mouth corner (smile)}}.
cloze.extra: Tip: Main smiling muscle.

cloze.text: Zygomaticus major attachments — insertion: {{c1::mouth corner}}; origin: {{c2::zygomatic bone}}.
Muscle of facial expression: {{c1::Zygomaticus major}} — main smiling muscle.
The {{c1::Zygomaticus minor}} (muscle of facial expression) — location: upper cheek to lip; action: {{c2::elevates upper lip}}.
cloze.extra: Tip: Assists sneering, showing upper teeth.

cloze.text: Zygomaticus minor attachments — insertion: {{c1::upper lip}}; origin: {{c2::zygomatic bone}}.
Muscle of facial expression: {{c1::Zygomaticus minor}} — assists sneering, showing upper teeth.
The {{c1::Levator labii superioris}} (muscle of facial expression) — location: beside nose; action: {{c2::raises upper lip}}.
cloze.extra: Tip: Exposes maxillary anterior teeth.

cloze.text: Levator labii superioris attachments — insertion: {{c1::upper lip}}; origin: {{c2::infraorbital rim of maxilla}}.
Muscle of facial expression: {{c1::Levator labii superioris}} — exposes maxillary anterior teeth.
The {{c1::Levator labii superioris alaeque nasi}} (muscle of facial expression) — location: alongside nose; action: {{c2::lifts upper lip and flares nostrils}}.
cloze.extra: Tip: Used in expressions of disgust.

cloze.text: Levator labii superioris alaeque nasi attachments — insertion: {{c1::upper lip and ala of nose}}; origin: {{c2::frontal process of maxilla}}.
Muscle of facial expression: {{c1::Levator labii superioris alaeque nasi}} — used in expressions of disgust.
The {{c1::Levator anguli oris}} (muscle of facial expression) — location: deep to zygomaticus; action: {{c2::lifts mouth corner}}.
cloze.extra: Tip: Deep elevator of smile.

cloze.text: Levator anguli oris attachments — insertion: {{c1::mouth corner}}; origin: {{c2::canine fossa of maxilla}}.
Muscle of facial expression: {{c1::Levator anguli oris}} — deep elevator of smile.
The {{c1::Risorius}} (muscle of facial expression) — location: cheek fascia to mouth corner; action: {{c2::retracts mouth corner horizontally}}.
cloze.extra: Tip: Creates fake or forced smile.

cloze.text: Risorius attachments — insertion: {{c1::mouth corner}}; origin: {{c2::fascia over masseter}}.
Muscle of facial expression: {{c1::Risorius}} — creates fake or forced smile.
The {{c1::Depressor anguli oris}} (muscle of facial expression) — location: lower chin; action: {{c2::pulls mouth corner downward}}.
cloze.extra: Tip: Used in frowning.

cloze.text: Depressor anguli oris attachments — insertion: {{c1::mouth corner}}; origin: {{c2::mandible}}.
Muscle of facial expression: {{c1::Depressor anguli oris}} — used in frowning.
The {{c1::Depressor labii inferioris}} (muscle of facial expression) — location: mandible to lower lip; action: {{c2::pulls lip down}}.
cloze.extra: Tip: Exposes mandibular anterior teeth.

cloze.text: Depressor labii inferioris attachments — insertion: {{c1::lower lip}}; origin: {{c2::mandible}}.
Muscle of facial expression: {{c1::Depressor labii inferioris}} — exposes mandibular anterior teeth.
The {{c1::Mentalis}} (muscle of facial expression) — location: chin; action: {{c2::raises and protrudes lower lip}}.
cloze.extra: Tip: Pouting muscle; creates chin dimples.

cloze.text: Mentalis attachments — insertion: {{c1::skin of chin}}; origin: {{c2::incisive fossa of mandible}}.
Muscle of facial expression: {{c1::Mentalis}} — pouting muscle; creates chin dimples.
The {{c1::Platysma}} (muscle of facial expression) — location: neck to lower face; action: {{c2::tenses neck, lowers jaw/mouth}}.
cloze.extra: Tip: Visible during stress or extreme tension.

cloze.text: Platysma attachments — insertion: {{c1::lower face skin}}; origin: {{c2::skin over clavicle and shoulder}}.
Muscle of facial expression: {{c1::Platysma}} — visible during stress or extreme tension.
All muscles of facial expression are innervated by the {{c1::facial (VII)}} nerve.
cloze.extra: Not printed on this page — standard fact added for contrast with the muscles of mastication (V).
